mcqs.question: Why can an immutable object still be seen in a corrupted state by another thread, if it's shared unsafely during construction?
options: Immutable objects cannot have construction-time bugs by definition
This can only happen if the object has a mutable field, which contradicts it being immutable
It can't -- immutability guarantees safe publication automatically in every language

Immutability only protects against mutation after the constructor returns; if a reference to the object leaks to another thread before construction finishes, that thread can observe a half-built object
mcqs.explanation: Publication safety is a separate concern from immutability -- immutability prevents races after the object exists, but a reference leaking out mid-construction lets another thread see an incomplete object before that guarantee even applies. This has nothing to do with mutable fields, and no language makes safe publication automatic just because a class is immutable.

mcqs.question: What does the static holder idiom (a private static nested class holding the singleton instance) rely on to guarantee thread-safe lazy initialization without an explicit lock?
options: The JVM's guarantee that a class is initialized exactly once, lazily, the first time it's referenced
The `synchronized` keyword applied automatically to every static field
A background thread that pre-creates the instance at JVM startup
The garbage collector preventing more than one instance from ever existing in memory
mcqs.explanation: The idiom leans entirely on the JVM's class-initialization guarantee -- exactly-once, lazy, and thread-safe by the language spec -- with no explicit lock needed. There's no automatic synchronized on static fields, no background pre-creation, and the garbage collector has no role in preventing duplicate instances.

mcqs.question: An LRU cache's hash map and recency list are protected by one shared lock instead of one lock per structure. Why?
options: Because most languages don't allow more than one lock per class
Because a single lock is always faster than two separate locks, regardless of the data
Because the map and list must always change together consistently; separate locks would let one update land without the other, leaving them inconsistent
Because the recency list doesn't actually need any synchronization
mcqs.explanation: When two structures must change together atomically, they need one shared lock -- separate locks would let a thread update one and get interrupted before updating the other, corrupting the invariant between them. There's no such per-class lock limit, a single lock isn't universally faster, and the recency list absolutely needs synchronization since it's mutated on every access.

mcqs.question: A class does `if (!cache.containsKey(k)) cache.put(k, expensiveCompute(k))` on top of a `ConcurrentHashMap`. Why is this still unsafe under concurrent access?
options: ConcurrentHashMap does not support both containsKey and put being called from the same class
The check-then-act sequence isn't atomic -- two threads can both see the key absent and both run expensiveCompute(k), even though each map operation individually is thread-safe
ConcurrentHashMap requires an explicit external lock for any use at all
expensiveCompute(k) can never be safely called from multiple threads
mcqs.explanation: The map's individual operations being thread-safe doesn't make a compound sequence built from them atomic -- two threads can interleave between the check and the act. There's no such restriction on calling both methods from one class, ConcurrentHashMap doesn't require external locking for basic safe use, and expensiveCompute itself may be perfectly safe to call concurrently -- the problem is duplicated, possibly inconsistent work, not an unsafe function.
